Nobody Wants This Lamborghini Gallardo, Low-Mileage Supercar Fails To Sell
14 photos
Photo: Cars&Bids
Can you believe it’s been more than two decades since Lamborghini unveiled the Gallardo ? Why, of course you can, as even though it may still be a stunning machine even by today’s standards, it was eventually replaced by the Huracan, which made way for the Temerario.
The Huracan was assembled from 2014 to 2024, and the Temerario, which is the Raging Bull’s new-age “baby” supercar, featuring a 4.0-liter twin-turbo plug-in hybrid V8, with 907 hp (920 ps/677 kW) combined, and 0-62 mph (0-100 kph) in 2.7 seconds, entered production at Sant’Agata Bolognese, Italy, in 2025.
Production of the Lamborghini Gallardo spanned from 2003 to 2013, and it is estimated that a little over 14,000 units were put together during this time. The lineup was vast, as it included the original Gallardo Coupe and Spyder, as well as the Superleggera, and the LP 560-4 Coupe and Spyder, LP 570-4 Superleggera, LP 570-4 Spyder Performante, LP 550-2 Coupe and Spyder, and others, which were part of the facelift that came out at the Geneva Motor Show back in 2008.
Pictured in the gallery is a 2009 Lamborghini Gallardo LP 560-4 Coupe, featuring an orange exterior and an orange and black interior. It’s registered in Calgary, AB, Canada, and it has a dealer behind it that reportedly bought it in September 2026, adding some 100 miles (~160 km) since. The vendor tried to part ways with it on Cars&Bids, yet when the online auction ended on November 10, 2026, the reserve was not met, so the supercar failed to change hands.
Photo: Cars&Bids More on that in a few moments, as first, we have to delve into some of its aspects, including the equipment. This Gallardo features 19-inch wheels, has green brake calipers, a transparent engine cover, and a nose-lift system to clear speed bumps and steep driveways easier. The dual-zone automatic climate control system and the leather upholstery are also mentioned in the ad.
There are also a few modifications on deck, such as the front and rear bumpers, as well as the floor mats and carpet covers. The chips and clearcoat cracks on the apron and rear diffuser, a pitting on the windshield, a chip on the roof panel, and a taillight bulb that needs to be replaced are some of the known flaws. This Lamborghini Gallardo also has wear on the driver’s seat and some interior plastic trim.
Moreover, the selling dealer also noted that the vehicle will lock/unlock automatically when the key fob is in proximity, and that the head unit display does not move anymore, so the access to the CD player is restricted. Thus, its next owner will have some things to sort out if they want their modern-classic supercar to return to its original shine.
Power is supplied by a V10 engine, as every petrolhead and their pet can tell you. The naturally aspirated mill has a 5.2-liter displacement, and in this case, it pumps out 552 hp (560 ps/412 kW) and 398 pound-feet (540 Nm) of torque. The engine drives all four wheels through a six-speed automated manual transmission. The 0-62 mph (0-100 kph) took 3.7 seconds when the car was new, and the top speed was 202 mph (325 kph).
Photo: Cars&Bids The listing shows that the supercar is accompanied by one key and that’s it, and that it is not eligible for import into the United States of America, and this is likely why it hasn’t got a lot of attention from bidders. After all, these things tend to fetch from $130,000 to $175,000 in our market these days, and cars with less than 20,000 miles (32,000 km) are considered low-mileage examples. This one checks this box, as it had 18,000 miles (29,000 km) on the odometer at the time of cataloging.
It is worth noting that this 2009 Lamborghini Gallardo LP 560-4 Coupe is still searching for a new home as we speak, after failing to change hands. The supercar was advertised on Cars&Bids as part of an online auction that recently ended (November 10, 2026), and it will be interesting to find out how much the vendor hopes to get from it. The highest bid was $68,000, and the reserve was not met.
So, if you are searching for a modern-classic “baby” supercar from Lamborghini that is considered a low-mileage example, albeit one that needs some work, with emphasis on the fact that you cannot import it to the States, then this one might just be the right machine for you. But assuming you were actually shopping for a cool Lamborghini Gallardo north of the US border and you came across this one, how much would you have paid for it?
You should check out this Lamborghini Gallardo in more detail here on the quoted website, though preferably after dropping a few lines below in the comments area.
